doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Composing at the piano and synthesizers
summary: She composes at the piano; tools do not dictate a composer's ideas.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Getting back a moment to your compositions, do you write at the piano, at a keyboard?
Yup I do, most of it. Sometimes ideas come to me on the horn, but for the most part, yeah I’m a piano thinker.
Do you have any kind of set-up in your apartment, a four track or any of that kind of gear?
All of the above, yeah. Yeah I’ve got a synthesizer keyboard and a JB 1080 which is a beautiful orchestral — a synthesizer with a lot of orchestral sounds on it. All kinds of tools to help.

Do you ever take a tune — you had mentioned the orchestral sounds and everything — you find a really great sound on the synthesizer, it’s really lush and it’s got all kinds of reverb and the whole thing — is there a danger in building a composition around a sound like that, that the melodic and harmonic content of the music may be kind of light? Do you ever take things back to the piano and see, does this thing stand on its own?

Oh absolutely. I mean if you’re a composer, the musical impulse comes from here. It’s not in your hands, it’s not in the sound. I think that’s what you’re getting at. The same criticism is often made about using electronics, it’s like a black box. That it dictates what © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

you do. But I think if you’re a true compositional thinker, the ideas come from here and translate through your use of sounds and whatever. But you should be very much in control of the musical materials, no matter what tools you’re using, whether it be a synthesizer or electronics or whatever, which are just as valid as playing an acoustic instrument, you know, it’s just how you do it, how you do it.
